metadata.title: vLLM.
metadata.note: Concept explainer (framework-first, built to pass PROOF). Topic named by request: vLLM, efficient LLM inference and serving. ONE reusable idea: LLM serving is MEMORY-bound, not compute-bound — the KV cache fills the GPU and caps throughput — and vLLM wins by treating the KV cache like an OS treats RAM: PagedAttention (page the cache into fixed-size blocks, allocate on demand, share) + continuous/iteration-level batching (swap requests in and out every step, keep the batch full). Transferable lesson the viewer keeps: memory-bound? stop reserving for the worst case — page it and keep the pipeline full. DOUBLE-CHECK LAW (facts verified, from the PagedAttention/vLLM SOSP'23 line of work and Orca OSDI'22 continuous batching): KV cache = per-token keys/values kept to avoid recompute, grows with tokens×concurrency, dominates dynamic GPU memory; naive contiguous per-request allocation sized for max length wastes ~60-80%; PagedAttention block-table paging cuts waste to <4% and enables copy-on-write block sharing for shared prefixes/parallel sampling; continuous batching admits/evicts per decode step vs static padding; net throughput gain is several× (headline ~2-4× over prior serving systems, up to ~24× over naive HF) — card/narration keep it qualitative ('several× / many times', same latency) to stay durable. Bookends render via remotion (ClaudeComposerAsk, ClaudeVerdictArtifact, ClaudeTitleOutro) at --scale=2 (4K); body B01-B04 are house-style 4K PIL cards (make_cards.py) — kinds versus, grid, example, versus.

beats.narration_text: Hey, I'm Muskan. You've got a strong open model and a GPU to serve it on, and yet under real traffic it's slow and you run out of memory almost immediately. vLLM is the serving engine that fixes this, often many times faster on the very same hardware. And the trick isn't a better model. It's treating memory the way an operating system does.

props.command: Same model, same GPU — so why can vLLM serve many times more traffic than a naive setup?
output: PagedAttention: KV cache like virtual memory
continuous batching keeps the GPU full

beats.narration_text: Start with where the time and memory actually go. When a model generates, it keeps a cache of every token it's seen, the keys and the values, so it doesn't recompute them. That's the KV cache, and it lives on the GPU. It grows with every token, and every request you serve at once. So what fills your GPU, and caps how many users you serve, isn't the math. It's this cache. Serving is a memory problem.

card.title: Math, or Memory?
card.subtitle: where the bottleneck really is
card.caption: the model keeps a cache of every token — that cache, not the math, fills the GPU

beats.narration_text: Here's how that memory gets wasted. The simple approach reserves one big, contiguous block per request, sized for the longest answer it might ever produce. But most answers are short, so most of that space is never touched, and the leftover gaps are too small to reuse. In practice, sixty to eighty percent of the KV memory sits idle. So only a handful of requests fit, and your expensive GPU spends most of its time waiting.

card.title: How The Memory Is Wasted.
card.subtitle: naive KV allocation

items.quote: the longest answer it might give

card.caption: reserve for the worst case and most of the GPU's memory sits empty

beats.narration_text: vLLM's answer is PagedAttention, borrowed straight from how your operating system handles memory. Instead of one big slab, it chops the KV cache into small, fixed-size blocks, handed out on demand, wherever there's room. A table maps each request's logical blocks to wherever they physically live. Waste drops to under four percent. And because blocks are just references, two requests sharing a prompt can share the same blocks, copying only when they diverge.

card.title: KV Cache, Paged.
card.subtitle: PagedAttention, borrowed from your OS
card.answer: fixed-size blocks, allocated on demand, non-contiguous → under 4% wasted · shared blocks for common prefixes
card.caption: a table maps each request's logical blocks to wherever they physically live

beats.narration_text: The second half is how requests are batched. The old way waits for a whole batch to finish together, padding everyone to the slowest, longest request, so the GPU stalls on the stragglers. vLLM schedules at the level of each step instead. The moment one request finishes, it leaves, and a waiting one takes its place, immediately. The batch stays full, every step. And more freed memory, from paging, means more requests can be in flight at once.

card.title: Static, or Continuous?
card.subtitle: how requests are batched
card.caption: iteration-level scheduling swaps requests in and out each step — no waiting on stragglers

beats.narration_text: So vLLM is really one idea applied twice: treat the KV cache like virtual memory. PagedAttention reclaims the memory you were wasting, and continuous batching keeps the GPU busy with it. Same model, same hardware, several times the throughput at the same latency. And the general lesson outlives the tool: when a system is memory-bound, stop reserving for the worst case. Page it, and keep the pipeline full.

props.artifactHeading: Treat the KV cache like virtual memory
artifactLines: LLM serving is memory-bound: the KV cache (every token's keys & values) fills the GPU and caps how many requests fit.
Naive serving reserves one contiguous slab per request, sized for the max answer — 60–80% sits idle.
PagedAttention pages the cache into fixed-size blocks, allocated on demand and shareable — waste drops below ~4%.
Continuous batching swaps requests in and out every step, so the freed memory keeps the GPU full: several× throughput, same latency.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Before you reach for a bigger GPU, ask one question: is my serving slow because of compute, or because of memory? And if it's memory, are you pre-allocating for a worst case that rarely happens? Because the fix might not be more hardware. It might be paging what you already have, and never letting the batch go half-empty.
